questions.q: A 2-day-old neonate presents with generalized blistering and erosions. Genetic testing reveals homozygous premature termination codons in COL7A1. Which of the following best explains the complete absence of Type VII collagen in this patient?
opts: Dominant-negative effect from structurally abnormal collagen dimers
Nonsense-mediated mRNA decay preventing translation of functional protein
Autosomal dominant inheritance pattern with heterozygous mutation
Delayed intracytoplasmic retention of collagen within basal keratinocytes
questions.exp: Homozygous or compound heterozygous premature termination codons (PTCs) in COL7A1 trigger nonsense-mediated mRNA decay, which degrades the aberrant mRNA and prevents synthesis of Type VII collagen. This mechanism accounts for the severe RDEB phenotype with complete collagen absence. The other options describe mechanisms seen in DDEB (dominant-negative), other inheritance patterns, or Bullous Dermolysis of the Newborn (intracytoplasmic retention).
questions.source: Dystrophic Epidermolysis Bullosa (COL7A1, Type VII Collagen)

questions.q: A term neonate is born with a taut, shiny, transparent parchment-like membrane covering the entire body. Within 3 weeks, the membrane peels off in sheets, revealing large, dark-brown, plate-like scales with severe ectropion and scarring alopecia. Which gene mutation is most likely responsible for this underlying disorder?
opts: ALOXE3 encoding lipoxygenase
TGM1 encoding transglutaminase-1
NIPAL4 encoding ichthyin
PNPLA1 encoding phospholipase
questions.exp:
The clinical presentation of large, dark-brown, plate-like scales in a bark-like mosaic pattern with severe ectropion and scarring alopecia is characteristic of lamellar ichthyosis (LI). The most common genetic cause of LI is an inactivating mutation in TGM1, which encodes transglutaminase-1, an enzyme critical for cornified cell envelope formation. ALOXE3, NIPAL4, and PNPLA1 mutations are associated with congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma (CIE), which presents with widespread erythroderma rather than plate-like scales.
🏰 Palace: Imagine a LAMINATED BROWN PLATE (LI) being glued together by TRANSGLUTAMINASE (TGM1)—the enzyme acts like industrial glue holding the bark-like scales in the castle's ancient chamber.

questions.q: A 4-year-old boy presents with fine, white-gray scales predominantly on his elbows and knees, with notably hyperlinear palms and a strong personal history of atopic dermatitis. His mother reports the rash began around age 6 months and worsens during winter. Histopathology shows orthohyperkeratosis with an absent stratum granulosum. Which genetic mutation most likely explains this presentation?
opts: Loss-of-function mutation in the FLG gene encoding filaggrin
Deletion of the STS gene on chromosome Xp22.3
Gain-of-function mutation in CTSC gene
Loss-of-function mutation in ABCA12 gene
questions.exp: Ichthyosis vulgaris is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the FLG gene on chromosome 1q21, which encodes filaggrin—a protein critical for keratin aggregation in the stratum granulosum and generation of natural moisturizing factors. The clinical presentation of fine scales on extensor surfaces sparing flexures, association with atopy, and pathognomonic absent stratum granulosum are diagnostic of IV, not other ichthyosis subtypes.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture FILAGGRIN as a FRAGILE LADDER (FLG) in the castle's STRATUM GRANULOSUM—when it breaks, moisture escapes and WINTER SCALES creep up the ELBOWS like winter ivy.

questions.q: A 3-day-old neonate presents with large, flaccid bullae on the diaper area that rupture within 24–48 hours, leaving moist erosions that dry into thin, golden-yellow crusts with a peripheral collarette of scale. The Nikolsky sign is negative and mucous membranes are spared. What is the histopathological cleavage plane and primary target antigen in this condition?
opts: Subcorneal acantholytic blister with cleavage in the stratum granulosum; target antigen is desmoglein 3 (Dsg3)
Subcorneal acantholytic blister with cleavage in the stratum granulosum; target antigen is desmoglein 1 (Dsg1)
Suprabasal acantholytic blister with cleavage beneath the basal layer; target antigen is desmoglein 1 (Dsg1)
Intradermal blister with cleavage in the papillary dermis; target antigen is desmoglein 1 (Dsg1)
questions.exp: Bullous impetigo is a staphylococcal exfoliative toxin–mediated disorder causing subcorneal acantholytic blisters due to cleavage of desmoglein 1 (Dsg1) in the stratum granulosum layer. Exfoliative toxins ETA and ETB, produced by phage group II S. aureus (types 71 and 55), act as trypsin-like serine proteases cleaving Dsg1 at this superficial level. Dsg3 is the target in pemphigus vulgaris, and suprabasal cleavage occurs in other acantholytic disorders.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a GOLDEN GATE BRIDGE (Dsg1) at the TOP FLOOR (stratum granulosum) of the castle, with a TOXIC STAPHYLOCOCCAL KNIGHT slicing through it—leaving the COLLARETTE MOAT around the broken gate below.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with multiple flat, flesh-colored papules on her trunk and extremities. She also has a history of recurrent upper respiratory infections with a breathy voice quality. Genetic testing reveals mutations in genes regulating cell-mediated immunity. Which HPV type is most likely responsible for her cutaneous and respiratory manifestations?
opts: HPV-2
HPV-3
HPV-8
HPV-16
questions.exp: HPV-3 causes flat (plane) warts and is strongly associated with Epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV), a genetic disorder with impaired cell-mediated immunity predisposing to widespread cutaneous HPV infection and potential respiratory involvement. HPV-2 causes common and mosaic warts without respiratory manifestations, HPV-8 is high-risk in EV but less associated with RRP, and HPV-16 is high-risk mucosal with SCC risk rather than flat warts.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a FLAT TIRE (HPV-3 flat warts) parked in front of a WHISPERING CASTLE (respiratory RRP) guarded by broken IMMUNITY GATES—the EV princess can't fight off the viral invaders.

questions.q: A histopathology slide from a sporotrichosis lesion shows yeast cells surrounded by a thick, star-shaped, radiating eosinophilic matrix. What is the immunological composition of this characteristic structure?
opts: Fungal cell wall polysaccharides and melanin
IgM and IgG antibodies deposited as part of the Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon
Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) and complement proteins
Host fibrin and collagen deposited around the organism
questions.exp: The asteroid body represents the Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon, an antigen-antibody complex composed of deposited IgM and IgG antibodies that form a protective matrix around the yeast cells. This structure serves to shield the yeast from host phagocytes.

questions.q: A 32-year-old HIV-positive male with CD4 count of 180 cells/mm³ presents with donovanosis. He is started on azithromycin 500 mg once daily, but after one week shows minimal clinical improvement with continued bleeding from the ulcer. What is the next most appropriate management step?
opts: Increase azithromycin dose to 1 g weekly instead of daily dosing
Switch to doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for better compliance
Add parenteral gentamicin (1 mg/kg IV or IM every 8 hours) to the oral regimen
Discontinue azithromycin and initiate TMP-SMX double-strength tablet twice daily
questions.exp: HIV co-infected patients with donovanosis experience more severe disease and significantly delayed healing; oral regimens alone often result in treatment failure in this population. Guidelines recommend an aggressive approach of adding parenteral gentamicin (1 mg/kg IV or IM every 8 hours) to the oral regimen for at least 3 weeks when there is no significant clinical improvement within the first few days to a week of oral therapy alone.

questions.q: According to modern dermatological classification, what is the critical distinction between 'Hypomelanosis of Ito' and 'Linear Nevoid Hypopigmentation'?
opts: Hypomelanosis of Ito has complete depigmentation, while Linear Nevoid Hypopigmentation shows only macular hypopigmentation
Hypomelanosis of Ito includes BOTH cutaneous pigmentation defects AND systemic/extracutaneous anomalies, while Linear Nevoid Hypopigmentation involves only the skin findings without internal defects
Hypomelanosis of Ito is autoimmune-mediated, while Linear Nevoid Hypopigmentation is genetic
Hypomelanosis of Ito predominantly affects males, while Linear Nevoid Hypopigmentation shows female predilection
questions.exp: By modern definition, Hypomelanosis of Ito is strictly reserved for patients with BOTH cutaneous hypopigmented lesions (tracing Blaschko's lines) AND systemic manifestations involving the CNS, musculoskeletal system, or eyes. Patients with only cutaneous findings are diagnosed as having Linear Nevoid Hypopigmentation instead.

questions.q: A 5-day-old term neonate with poor perineal hygiene develops fever, irritability, and extreme cutaneous tenderness followed by faint macular erythema with flexural accentuation. Within 48 hours, widespread wrinkling and tissue-paper-like appearance develops. Blood cultures are negative, but Gram-positive cocci are isolated from the umbilical stump. What is the pathophysiological mechanism distinguishing this generalized presentation from localized bullous impetigo?
opts: Direct cutaneous infection with S. aureus in multiple body sites simultaneously
Hematogenous dissemination of exfoliative toxins (ETA/ETB) from a distant, often occult primary focus, causing systemic rather than localized Dsg1 cleavage
Altered host immunity allowing disseminated S. aureus bacteremia with secondary cutaneous seeding
Increased susceptibility of the neonatal epidermis to toxin due to immature barrier function rather than toxin-mediated mechanism
questions.exp: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS/Ritter's disease) differs from localized bullous impetigo in that exfoliative toxins act systemically, diffusing hematogenously from an occult primary focus (e.g., omphalitis, conjunctivitis, or colonized umbilical stump) to produce widespread Dsg1 cleavage, whereas bullous impetigo results from local toxin production at the infection site. Blood cultures are typically negative in SSSS because the bacteremia is minimal; the pathology is toxin-mediated, not bacteremia-driven.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine a TOXIC POISON (ETA/ETB toxin) PUMPED THROUGH THE CASTLE'S BLOOD PLUMBING (hematogenous spread), reaching every GOLDEN GATE BRIDGE (Dsg1) in the GRAND HALLS (entire skin), while the original SOURCE SITS HIDDEN IN THE DUNGEON (occult omphalitis)—leaving TISSUE-PAPER WRINKLES everywhere the poison flows.

questions.q: A 2-month-old Caucasian female infant presents with a rapidly enlarging bright red nodule on the upper lip crossing the vermilion border. The parents are counselled regarding complications and systemic therapy options. What is the female-to-male ratio of infantile haemangioma incidence, and which genetic locus has been mapped as a susceptibility factor in familial cases?
opts: F:M ratio 1:2; chromosome 3p
F:M ratio 2:1–5:1; chromosome 5q
F:M ratio 3:1; chromosome 7q
F:M ratio 1:1; chromosome 10q
questions.exp: Infantile haemangiomas show a pronounced female predominance with an F:M ratio of 2:1 to 5:1, and familial cases with autosomal dominant transmission have been linked to chromosome 5q via linkage studies. Loss of heterozygosity at 5q is also observed in sporadic cases, establishing this locus as a key susceptibility region.

questions.q: A neonate is suspected to have epidermolysis bullosa (EB) and requires initial assessment. According to EB supportive care principles, where should this assessment ideally occur to prevent iatrogenic skin trauma?
opts: At the regional pediatric dermatology center after transport
At the birthing unit by an EB clinical nurse specialist
At the neonatal intensive care unit after stabilization
At the general pediatric ward following routine neonatal screening
questions.exp: EB neonates have extraordinarily fragile skin that is easily damaged by mechanical trauma. Initial assessment should occur at the birthing unit by an EB clinical nurse specialist to avoid iatrogenic skin stripping during unnecessary transportation. This prevents preventable blistering and skin loss in these highly vulnerable patients.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 9] supportive care principles, EB Nurse role

questions.q: During upper eyelid blepharoplasty marking, what is the minimum distance that must be maintained between the upper limit of skin excision and the superior orbital margin to prevent complications?
opts: At least 5 mm
At least 10 mm
At least 15 mm
At least 20 mm
questions.exp: The upper limit of excision must be maintained at least 10 mm from the superior orbital margin to avoid injury to deeper structures and preserve normal eyelid function. This distance ensures adequate tissue remains for proper closure and prevents retraction complications.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: Picture a GUARD standing 10 MILLIMETERS from the CASTLE'S UPPER WALL—closer and the tower collapses (retraction), further and you waste good stone (over-excision).

questions.q: A 3-year-old girl presents with asymmetric, bizarre whorls and streaks of hypopigmentation on her trunk and extremities that follow the lines of Blaschko. She also has intellectual disability and seizures. Which of the following correctly describes the pathophysiological basis of this condition?
opts: Autoimmune destruction of melanocytes mediated by pathogenic anti-melanocyte antibodies
Post-zygotic somatic mutations occurring early in embryogenesis leading to a clone of pigment-deficient skin cells
HLA-associated T-cell mediated immune complex deposition in the dermal-epidermal junction
X-linked inheritance pattern identical to Incontinentia Pigmenti (Bloch-Sulzberger syndrome)
questions.exp: Hypomelanosis of Ito is a genetic mosaicism and neurocutaneous dysplasia caused by post-zygotic somatic mutations in early embryogenesis, not an autoimmune disorder. It has no autoimmune serology associations, pathogenic antibodies, or HLA links, and is genetically completely unrelated to Incontinentia Pigmenti despite the historical misnomer 'Incontinentia Pigmenti Achromians.'

questions.q: A 28-year-old male with a history of genital condylomata is counseled regarding malignant transformation risk. His HPV serology is positive for types 6 and 11. Which molecular mechanism best explains his relatively low cancer risk despite mucosal HPV infection?
opts: E6 and E7 genes are constitutively expressed due to E2 gene deletion
Viral DNA remains as an extrachromosomal episome with intact E2 repression of E6/E7
Integration into the host genome increases p53 degradation capacity
E6 protein binds weakly to p53, leading to complete loss of tumor suppression
questions.exp: Low-risk HPV types (6, 11) maintain their DNA as extrachromosomal episomes that do not integrate into the host genome, preserving the E2 gene which remains functionally intact and tightly represses E6 and E7 oncogene expression. High-risk types integrate, delete E2, and cause uncontrolled E6/E7 expression leading to p53 degradation and malignant transformation.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine LOW-RISK HPV as a HAPPY CIRCULAR FRISBEE (episome) floating freely outside the CASTLE GATES (genome), while a STRONG GATEKEEPER E2 (with intact gene) blocks the E6/E7 ASSASSINS from entering the p53 THRONE ROOM—but HIGH-RISK HPV breaks through the gates and stabs the king.

questions.q: A 6-month-old child with severe generalized epidermolysis bullosa has extensive denuded skin areas and a fever of 38.5°C. Which of the following represents the most appropriate first-line intervention to reduce bacterial colonization and prevent sepsis?
opts: Immediate oral broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy with amoxicillin-clavulanate
Daily bathing in dilute sodium hypochlorite (bleach) soaks (~0.005%) or 0.25% acetic acid soaks
Prophylactic intravenous vancomycin and ceftazidime pending culture results
Aggressive daily topical antibiotic ointment (mupirocin) application to all denuded areas
questions.exp: First-line bacterial management in EB involves routine bathing or soaking in dilute sodium hypochlorite (~0.005%) or 0.25% acetic acid to safely reduce bacterial colonization without inducing antimicrobial resistance. Systemic antibiotics and chronic topical antibiotics are reserved for proven, cultured clinical infections only, as overuse promotes multidrug-resistant pathogens.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 9] supportive care principles, EB Nurse role

questions.q: A 12-year-old boy with severe generalized RDEB (Hallopeau-Siemens variant) develops progressive fusion of fingers into a cocoon-like encasement with inability to extend digits. What is the pathological basis underlying this 'mitten deformity' or pseudosyndactyly?
opts: Acute inflammation and vasculitis in the sublamina densa zone
Progressive atrophic scarring and contracture formation from complete absence of Type VII collagen and anchoring fibrils
Autoimmune destruction of keratinocyte adhesion molecules in the epidermis
Genetic deletion of genes encoding actin-binding proteins in the basal layer
questions.exp: Pseudosyndactyly in severe RDEB results from profound atrophic scarring and progressive flexion contractures due to the complete absence of Type VII collagen and anchoring fibrils, which normally stabilize the dermal-epidermal junction. Recurrent blistering and severe scarring lead to digit fusion. This pathognomonic deformity is a hallmark of Hallopeau-Siemens RDEB and reflects the fundamental structural defect in the sublamina densa zone.
questions.source: Dystrophic Epidermolysis Bullosa (COL7A1, Type VII Collagen)

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman has had a pathognomonic heliotrope rash and Gottron papules for 8 months. Muscle enzyme levels are normal, electromyography is normal, and MRI of the thighs shows no myositis. She reports no subjective muscle weakness. Which diagnostic classification best describes her condition?
opts: Polymyositis with early muscle involvement
Amyopathic dermatomyositis (CADM)
Hypomyopathic dermatomyositis (CADM)
Possible dermatomyositis by ENMC criteria
questions.exp: This patient presents with hallmark DM skin manifestations (heliotrope rash and Gottron papules) for >6 months but has entirely normal muscle enzymes, normal EMG, and normal muscle imaging with no clinical muscle weakness. This defines amyopathic DM, a subset of clinically amyopathic dermatomyositis (CADM) recognized by Sontheimer. Hypomyopathic DM would require subclinical evidence of myositis on laboratory testing or imaging despite absent clinical muscle symptoms.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: AMYOPATHIC = NO muscles affected (a-myo-pathic = no muscle disease)—perfect skin rash, ZERO enzyme elevation, ZERO EMG findings—like a beautiful castle exterior with a completely healthy interior; HYPO-myopathic = muscles are subclinically sneaky with hidden lab/imaging damage despite no weakness.

questions.q: A 6-week-old premature female infant (birth weight 850 g) presents with multiple small red macules on the trunk and face. On examination, the lesions blanch with pressure. Blood tests reveal hepatomegaly. Which immunohistochemical marker would definitively confirm the diagnosis of infantile haemangioma rather than a vascular malformation?
opts: CD34 positivity in endothelial cells
GLUT1 (glucose transporter-1) positivity throughout all phases of the lesion
Factor VIII-related antigen expression
Smooth muscle actin positivity in vessel walls
questions.exp: GLUT1 is the definitive immunohistochemical hallmark of infantile haemangiomas, universally expressed by tumour endothelial cells in proliferating, involuting, and involuted phases, thereby distinguishing IH from congenital haemangiomas and vascular malformations which lack this marker. The patient's risk profile (prematurity, low birth weight <1000 g, female gender) places her in the 25–30% incidence group for IH in this weight category.

questions.q: Which mechanism of action best explains how glycolic acid (a commonly used alpha-hydroxy acid) produces its peeling effect?
opts: Protein coagulation causing cellular necrosis in the epidermis and dermis
Lysis of corneodesmosomes to accelerate keratinocyte turnover and cell shedding
Direct inhibition of tyrosinase enzyme activity in melanocytes
Activation of fibroblast proliferation without any exfoliative effect
questions.exp: Glycolic acid works through a keratolytic mechanism by interfering with the bonds (corneodesmosomes) holding cells together, which accelerates keratinocyte turnover and promotes shedding. Protein coagulation is the mechanism of TCA and phenol; tyrosinase inhibition is seen with hydroquinone and kojic acid; and fibroblast activation occurs as part of dermal remodeling but is not the primary peeling mechanism.

questions.q: A 52-year-old woman presents with symmetric proximal muscle weakness and a violaceous rash on the knuckles, eyelids, and chest. Muscle enzymes are markedly elevated, and EMG shows myopathic features. Which pathogenic mechanism best distinguishes her dermatomyositis from polymyositis?
opts: CD8+ cytotoxic T-cell-mediated direct myocyte destruction
Humorally mediated microangiopathy with capillary damage
Autoantibody-independent complement activation in muscle fiber sarcolemma
IgA immune complex deposition in the dermis and subcutis
questions.exp: Dermatomyositis is fundamentally a humorally mediated microangiopathy, whereas polymyositis is primarily driven by CD8+ T-cell-mediated myocyte destruction. This distinction was a major paradigm shift from the older Bohan and Peter criteria, which grouped DM and PM together. Understanding this pathogenic difference is crucial for comprehending the distinct clinical and immunological profiles of these two idiopathic inflammatory myopathies.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine HUMORAL antibodies (liquid gold coins) raining down on TINY BLOOD VESSEL capillaries in the castle moat—DM's watery, vascular destruction—while PM's T-cells are SOLID WARRIORS stabbing muscle fibers directly on the ramparts.

questions.q: A 45-year-old gardener from Brazil presents with painful nodular lesions along the forearm following a cat scratch 3 weeks ago. Culture at 37°C shows small cigar-shaped budding yeasts measuring 4 μm. Which Sporothrix species is most likely responsible for this zoonotic transmission pattern?
opts: Sporothrix schenckii sensu stricto
Sporothrix brasiliensis
Sporothrix globosa
Sporothrix mexicana
questions.exp: Sporothrix brasiliensis is the highly virulent species responsible for the massive zoonotic epidemic in Brazil, transmitted specifically via bites and scratches from infected cats. The other species are not associated with this cat-mediated transmission route or are less common in causing epidemic disease.

questions.q: A pregnant woman at 30 weeks' gestation presents with polyhydramnios and markedly decreased fetal movements on ultrasound. Fetal skin biopsy via cordocentesis shows profound dermal immaturity with failed collagen and elastic fiber organization. The family history reveals the parents are consanguineous Dutch-German Mennonites. Which genetic inheritance pattern and prognosis is most likely?
opts: Autosomal dominant de novo mutation; 50% survival to adulthood with surgical intervention
Autosomal recessive ZMPSTE24 mutation; invariably fatal within the first week of life
X-linked recessive laminopathy; variable survival depending on X-inactivation patterns
Mitochondrial inheritance; progressive deterioration over months with supportive care
questions.exp: Restrictive dermopathy caused by ZMPSTE24 mutations follows autosomal recessive inheritance and is invariably fatal within the first week of life due to respiratory insufficiency from pulmonary hypoplasia and severe chest wall restriction. The Old Colony Mennonite and Hutterite populations have a documented founder mutation with exceptionally high carrier frequency (up to 1 in 21 in some South Dakota Hutterite communities), making consanguineous families in this population at high risk. There is no known intervention that improves survival.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: MENNONITE CASTLE holds a DEADLY FOUNDER MUTATION—autosomal RECESSIVE like locked iron doors. Babies born stiff as armor, lungs too small to inflate, dead within WEEK ONE. No escape, no cure. The rarest 60 cases in medical history, all grim endings.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman with significant photodamage and acne scars presents for skin rejuvenation. You decide to perform a chemical peel that will achieve necrosis extending through the papillary dermis. Which agent and concentration should you use?
opts: Glycolic acid 30–50%
Baker-Gordon phenol formula
questions.exp: Medium-depth peels achieve necrosis at or through the level of the papillary dermis and are indicated for photodamage and scars. TCA 35–40% is the standard medium-depth agent, while TCA 10–20% is superficial, glycolic acid 30–50% is superficial, and Baker-Gordon phenol achieves deep peeling into the reticular dermis.

questions.q: An 8-year-old boy with X-linked recessive ichthyosis presents with thick, dark-brown, tightly adherent scales on his neck, preauricular region, and lateral face—creating a characteristic 'dirty neck' appearance. Which of the following distinguishes this condition from ichthyosis vulgaris?
opts: Involvement of flexural areas and complete sparing of palms/soles, with steroid sulfatase deficiency
Fine white scales exclusively on extensor surfaces with hyperlinear palms and soles
Autosomal dominant inheritance with onset at birth
Primary defect in gap junction protein connexin 30
questions.exp: Recessive X-linked ichthyosis is caused by STS gene deletion leading to steroid sulfatase deficiency and cholesterol sulfate accumulation. Unlike ichthyosis vulgaris (which spares flexures and palms/soles), RXLI characteristically involves flexures and lateral face while completely sparing palms and soles. The dark-brown, adherent scales and 'dirty neck' appearance are hallmark features.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine STEROID SULFATE (STS) as SLUDGY TARRY SCALES choking the castle's FLEXURAL MOAT and DIRTY NECK WALLS—while the ROYAL PALMS remain pristine and untouched.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman with donovanosis presents with an active genital ulcer. She responds well to azithromycin therapy and the ulcer becomes completely re-epithelialized after 3 weeks of treatment. She asks when she can stop her medication. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Stop azithromycin immediately after lesion re-epithelialization at 3 weeks
Continue azithromycin for an extended period beyond lesion healing to prevent relapse
Switch to doxycycline for an additional 2 weeks after healing
Stop azithromycin but start ciprofloxacin as maintenance therapy
questions.exp: Donovanosis requires prolonged treatment extending beyond initial healing, as early cessation results in high relapse rates occurring 6–18 months after apparently effective therapy. Guidelines recommend continuing treatment for some time after lesions have completely healed and re-epithelialized. Azithromycin's prolonged tissue half-life of 68 hours and excellent intracellular accumulation make it ideal for reaching macrophages where Klebsiella granulomatis resides.

questions.q: A 32-year-old patient presents with isolated lower eyelid puffiness from orbital fat herniation and mild dark circles, but has no skin laxity or orbital muscle hypertrophy. Which lower lid blepharoplasty approach is most appropriate?
opts: Transcutaneous approach with full skin excision
Transconjunctival approach with fat trimming
Combined approach with levator advancement
Open sky approach with septoplasty
questions.exp: Transconjunctival blepharoplasty is ideal for younger patients with isolated orbital fat herniation (baggy eyes and dark circles) who have minimal or no skin wrinkling or laxity. This approach provides direct access to fat without external scarring and avoids the higher ectropion risk associated with transcutaneous dissection in patients without skin laxity.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: YOUNG PATIENT = TRANSCONJUNCTIVAL (secret back-door entry), OLDER PATIENT = TRANSCUTANEOUS (needs front-door for skin removal). No wrinkles? Hide the incision INSIDE the eyelid like treasure behind tapestries.

questions.q: A premature newborn presents with the classic collodion baby phenotype. What is the approximate percentage of collodion babies that will subsequently develop a nonsyndromic autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis (ARCI) after membrane shedding?
questions.exp:
The collodion baby phenotype represents the initial cutaneous manifestation of several congenital disorders of cornification. Approximately 80% to 90% of collodion babies will shed their membrane and evolve into a form of nonsyndromic ARCI, most commonly either lamellar ichthyosis or congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma. The remaining 10% to 20% may progress to other genodermatoses or represent self-healing collodion babies.
🏰 Palace: Picture 80-90 ARCI KNIGHTS marching out of a COLLODION CASTLE gate in formation—the vast majority transformation from the plastic wrap phenotype into ichthyosis variants.

questions.q: A newborn presents with profound skin rigidity, tightly adherent skin, and respiratory insufficiency requiring intubation. Genetic testing reveals homozygous mutations in the ZMPSTE24 gene. Which of the following best describes the molecular consequence of this mutation?
opts: Loss of lamin A and lamin C structural proteins directly
Failure to cleave and process farnesylated prelamin A into mature lamin A, causing toxic accumulation at the nuclear envelope
Autoimmune-mediated destruction of the nuclear lamina via HLA-driven mechanisms
Defective dermal collagen cross-linking due to impaired lysyl oxidase activity
questions.exp: ZMPSTE24 encodes a zinc metallopeptidase responsible for post-translational cleavage and processing of farnesylated prelamin A into mature lamin A. Without functional ZMPSTE24, unprocessed toxic prelamin A accumulates at the nuclear envelope, structurally damaging the nuclear lamina and disrupting DNA replication and transcription. This is a secondary laminopathy (as opposed to primary LMNA mutations), and restrictive dermopathy is a monogenic Mendelian disorder with no HLA associations.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: Picture a ZMPSTE24 BOUNCER at the castle gate—he's supposed to CUT (cleave) toxic farnesylated prelamin A bouncers into safe mature lamin A guests. Without him, toxic bouncers pile up, wreck the nuclear envelope doors, and the whole castle (skin) locks up rigid and lethal.
